content.p: At about 4:45 in the afternoon of 7 January 2021, a home security camera recorded May Millete, known to almost everyone as Maya, walking into her house in the Eastlake area of Chula Vista, south of San Diego. No camera ever recorded her leaving. She was 39, a civilian worker on a Navy base, and the mother of three children. That afternoon she had phoned two law firms about a divorce. Two days later the family was due to drive to Big Bear for her daughter's birthday.

Her body has never been found. Her husband, Larry Millete, was arrested nine months later and charged with her murder. On 9 July 2026, after a trial built entirely on circumstantial evidence, a jury in Chula Vista convicted him of first-degree murder. Prosecutors argued that he killed her because she was leaving him, and pointed to months of spending on online "spell casters" whose services he asked, in the end, to make her sick or helpless. He has denied killing her, and his lawyers are preparing to challenge the verdict.

Maya, a former Hawaii resident who graduated from Radford High School there, met Larry when they were both 15 and married him at 18. He worked at the Naval Medical Center in San Diego; she worked as a civilian for the Department of Defense. By 2020, family members later said, the marriage was in serious trouble. The couple tried counselling and separated for several weeks that year. Her sister Maricris Drouaillet, who saw them on a camping trip over the New Year of 2021, remembered a lot of arguing.

Investigators found that from September 2020 Maya had been in near-daily contact with a married co-worker, in messages that a district attorney's investigator described as sexual and emotional. She kept the affair from her family. In a recording she secretly made of one argument, Larry accused her of it. At the preliminary hearing Maya's sister-in-law testified that Maya had told her Larry punched the wall when he got angry. A co-worker testified that Maya had told her, in tears, that she was afraid Larry would hurt the children to hurt her. Drouaillet and the same sister-in-law both testified that Maya had told them that if anything happened to her, it would be Larry.

The strangest evidence came from Larry Millete's own email. Investigators found hundreds of messages to online companies that sold "spells". He told a reporter he had started with books on love languages, therapy and a pastor before finding love spells on the internet, and that he believed in them. In September 2020 he asked one seller: "Please help me. I want her to fall madly in love with me again." He even left one of them a review, saying that his casting had not yet manifested but that he was counting on it.

According to the arrest warrant and the prosecution, the requests changed over the months that followed: from making Maya love him again, to making her obey him, to making her ill or incapacitated so that she would depend on him and could not leave. He also asked for harm to come to the man she had been seeing. The night before she vanished, prosecutors said, he asked what a spell would cost to make his wife change her mind about divorcing him. At 9 a.m. on 7 January he wrote to another seller that the divorce was going to happen whether he wanted it or not, and at 3 p.m., to a third: "I'm shaking inside ready to snap." He also texted his boss that day, "I'm about to lose it." Two days earlier he had told the same boss, "She's asking for a divorce again." The spell requests against Maya stopped after she disappeared. Two days later, prosecutors said, he asked one seller to stop hexing his wife and to hex the other man instead.
content.h2: The night and the next day
content.p: Maya came home from a car wash on the afternoon of 7 January. According to trial testimony, her last contact with anyone was a text exchange with one of her sisters at about 8:15 that evening. At about 1:25 a.m. on 8 January her phone dropped off the cellular network for good.

At 5:59 a.m. a neighbour's camera showed the family's Lexus SUV pulling out and then reversing into the garage. About 45 minutes later it drove away with Larry and their youngest child inside, and it did not come back until just after 6 p.m. His phone was off for much of that time, something detectives said he rarely did. He told a detective he had taken his son to Torrey Pines, but lifeguards there did not remember them, and beach car park cameras did not record the SUV. Data from the car showed the home address entered into its navigation system at 3:29 p.m., two and a half hours before they got back, which suggested, NBC 7 reported, that they were coming back from somewhere much farther away. Prosecutors later said they believed he drove into the desert east of San Diego County and buried her there.

Maya's family could not reach her. Larry, her siblings later testified, behaved as if nothing was wrong, so at 11:18 p.m. on 9 January Drouaillet called the police herself. Officers arrived at about 1 a.m. and learned that Maya had not been seen for three days. Her car was still at the house.

For months, volunteers combed the hills near the house and the area around Mount San Miguel Park every weekend, and the family plastered Chula Vista with posters. Larry did not join them. About a month in, he hired a lawyer and stopped cooperating with police. Police searched the house on 23 January, again on 7 May and again in July. By April detectives had interviewed 55 people and written 16 search warrants, and the FBI, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the district attorney had formally joined the case. A neighbour's security camera had recorded several bangs on the night she was believed to have vanished; police said they had received no report of gunshots and analysed the recording.

In May 2021 a court issued a temporary gun violence restraining order against Larry, and officers carried what appeared to be rifles and ammunition boxes out of the house. On 21 July, at a hearing on that order, police named him for the first time as a person of interest. That spring, at about 8 p.m. one evening, a neighbour had seen a lone man she believed was Larry beside a large fire in the Milletes' backyard pit, and police later recovered a burned credit card and papers. Larry said the family had burned junk mail for years.

On 19 October 2021 Chula Vista police arrested him. District Attorney Summer Stephan said Maya had been killed after she contacted a divorce lawyer, and argued that the missing body was itself evidence of murder: a person who dies by suicide, she said, cannot conceal their own remains. He was charged with murder and with illegal possession of an assault rifle, and pleaded not guilty. Within days a judge barred him from contacting his children after prosecutors said he had made 129 calls from jail to his parents' home, where they were living, and had told two of them to watch a violent film about prison life.

The case then moved slowly. His mental competence was questioned in 2022 and confirmed. A long preliminary hearing ended in January 2024 with an order that he stand trial. His first lawyer left the case in 2023, saying he could no longer pay. The trial was postponed several times, and a request to move it out of Chula Vista because of the publicity was refused. In August 2024 a judge gave custody of the three children to Drouaillet, who had been fighting Larry's parents for it.

In a series of jailhouse interviews with NBC 7 in 2023, against his lawyer's advice, Larry Millete called the allegations outrageous and said he still believed Maya was alive. He declined to say where he had gone on 8 January, and suggested that witnesses had been coerced. Asked why he had not joined the searches, he said he had received death threats and that he shed tears in private.

After repeated delays the trial was set for 11 May 2026. It lasted about seven weeks, with more than 60 witnesses. Bowles admitted that she could not say how Maya had died, but argued that Larry was the only person with both the motive and the means. She portrayed him as possessive and controlling: he tracked his wife's movements, controlled the family money and, when all else failed, paid strangers on the internet to bend her will. She pointed to Maya's plans for the year ahead and her devotion to her children as proof that she had not simply walked away. The absence of a body, she said, showed a crime "so well-planned that it is nothing other than premeditation."

One possible method was raised. After his arrest investigators found a vial in the house whose contents tested positive for coniine, the poison in hemlock, and he had searched online many times for poison hemlock and for other ways to kill or incapacitate a person. His lawyer, Liann Sabatini, called the poison theory "silly". Hemlock grows all over San Diego County, she said; one of the children could have picked it, and a guilty man would hardly have kept it in the house almost a year later. She said his searches reflected thoughts of suicide as his marriage fell apart.

Sabatini told the jury that what the prosecution called stalking was a heartbroken husband's "tragic investigation" into whether his wife was cheating, and that Maya had "gaslit" him by denying the affair and casting him as the villain. "There is no playbook for heartbreak," she said. The jurors, she argued, were being asked to speculate in a case with no body, no crime scene, no weapon and no eyewitness.

The jury deliberated for less than a day, about five hours by most accounts, before convicting Larry Millete, then 44, of first-degree murder on 9 July 2026. "Finally, justice has been served for Maya," Stephan said. Drouaillet, who had organised searches for her younger sister for five years, said the family's work was not finished. "We still have to bring my sister home, to bring her to her three children," she said.

The weapons charge had been kept separate from the murder trial. On 20 July he pleaded guilty to possessing an assault weapon, which carries up to three years, and sentencing on both counts was set for 29 September. On that day his lawyers asked for more time. They had subpoenaed trial transcripts and local television stations' full interviews with jurors, apparently to support a motion for a new trial or an appeal. Over the prosecution's objection, Judge Enrique Camarena moved sentencing to 2 November 2026. Murder in the first degree carries 25 years to life. He has been in custody since October 2021, and that time will count towards his sentence.
Maya Millete is still missing. Her friends were planning another search for October.
